screens.title: Troubleshooting PAP

claims.text: Troubleshooting PAP
claims.ciasQuote: Section III: Troubleshooting CPAP Below, find our advice for how to address common issues with CPAP.
claims.note: CPAP renamed PAP (app-wide convention).

claims.text: This module offers practical guidance for common PAP problems.
claims.ciasQuote: Section III: Troubleshooting CPAP Below, find our advice for how to address common issues with CPAP.

claims.text: Discuss persistent concerns with the healthcare provider or equipment team.
claims.ciasQuote: Talk to the healthcare provider that prescribed your CPAP machine to help you troubleshoot these issues. | it’s important to work with your healthcare provider and the medical equipment company to find your fit
claims.note: CIAS refers to prescribing provider; equipment company named on p20.

claims.text: Start by checking one category at a time: mask fit, tubing and connections, humidification, nasal comfort, or the device data.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p20
claims.ciasQuote: The machine will give data on sleep quality and duration and on how effective the CPAP is in treating the events.
claims.note: Method is app-authored. Categories loosely mirror Section III topics; device data mentioned only on p20. "Tubing and connections" is not a CIAS topic.

claims.text: Small, supported changes are easier to evaluate than changing several things at once.
claims.note: App-authored process guidance.

claims.text: This app cannot diagnose a problem or prescribe a setting.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p10
claims.ciasQuote: only a physician can determine the pressure amount needed
claims.note: App disclaimer; consistent with CIAS p10 (only a physician sets pressure).

claims.text: If a problem repeatedly prevents PAP use, ask the prescribing provider or equipment team for help.
claims.ciasQuote: Talk to the healthcare provider that prescribed your CPAP machine to help you troubleshoot these issues.

claims.text: Seek prompt medical care for severe or rapidly worsening symptoms.
claims.note: Generic safety-net line; Section III has none. Include in clinical sign-off of safety wording.

claims.text: Use the manufacturer instructions for your particular mask and device.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p23
claims.ciasQuote: Check your machine’s manual for instructions on cleaning and frequency.
claims.note: CIAS says check the manual only for cleaning; the app generalizes it to all mask and device use.

claims.text: Write down when the problem starts, what it feels like, and what you already tried.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p20
claims.ciasQuote: Keeping a diary to write down your symptoms before starting therapy, such as sleepiness, daytime naps, insomnia.
claims.note: CIAS diary (p20) is for symptoms before starting therapy, not a troubleshooting log.

screens.narrationNote: EN narrationText equals paragraphs + keyPoints, in order, word for word. ES narrationText also matches its own visible text.
spanishNotes: Structure, keyPoints and narration match. "equipo de equipos médicos" (equipment team) is awkward wording, repeated across screens; meaning kept.

screens.title: My Mask Feels Too Tight or Uncomfortable

claims.text: My Mask Feels Too Tight or Uncomfortable
claims.ciasQuote: What if the mask feels uncomfortable or is pressing too hard on my face?

claims.text: The mask should not need to be painfully tight or leave persistent facial marks.
claims.ciasQuote: The mask should not be too tight on the face or leave long lasting facial marks in the morning after nightly use.
claims.note: Threshold drift: CIAS says "too tight"; the app says "painfully tight", which suggests tight-but-not-painful is fine. Whether this matters is a clinical call.

claims.text: Adjusting straps may help while maintaining a seal.
claims.ciasQuote: You can try loosening the straps and seeing if you continue to have a good seal.
claims.note: CIAS specifically says loosening; app says "adjusting".

claims.text: If it only seals when extremely tight, ask about another mask style.
claims.ciasQuote: If it needs to be very tight for adequate seal, talk to your healthcare provider about trying a different type of mask.
claims.note: CIAS names the healthcare provider as the person to ask; app leaves it unspecified in this sentence.

claims.text: With the machine running, gently reseat the mask and adjust one strap at a time.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: The goal is a seal that stays in place without painful pressure; overtightening can make pressure points and leaks worse.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p21
claims.ciasQuote: You may need to play around with adjusting the straps to ensure a fit where the mask stays in place or prevents a leak.
claims.note: "Stays in place" echoes CIAS p21; the claim that overtightening worsens pressure points and leaks is not in CIAS.

claims.text: If comfort remains poor, ask the equipment team to check the size, cushion, headgear, and mask style.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p20
claims.ciasQuote: it’s important to work with your healthcare provider and the medical equipment company to find your fit
claims.note: Section III routes to the healthcare provider; size/cushion/headgear check is app-added. p20 supports working with the equipment company.

claims.text: Nasal pillows, a nasal mask, and a full-face mask distribute contact differently.
claims.ciasQuote: For example, a nasal pillow type mask might reduce skin contact and be easier to use for you.
claims.note: Generalizes the CIAS example that nasal pillows may reduce skin contact.

claims.text: Fit the mask with airflow on and use the smallest adjustment that improves the seal.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: Ask for a refit when the mask only works if it is painfully tight.
claims.ciasQuote: If it needs to be very tight for adequate seal, talk to your healthcare provider about trying a different type of mask.
claims.note: CIAS: if it must be "very tight", ask the healthcare provider about a different type of mask. App: if "painfully tight", ask for a refit. Both the threshold and the action differ slightly.

screens.narrationNote: EN narrationText equals paragraphs + keyPoints, in order, word for word. ES narrationText also matches its own visible text.
spanishNotes: P1 s2 "Ajustar las correas puede ayudar a mantener un sello" reads as "adjusting straps can help maintain a seal"; EN means adjusting (loosening) may help while still keeping the seal. Minor drift.
mediaNotes: image-registry m9-02-mask-adjustment.jpg: alt text accurate. Looks like manufacturer product photography; attribution "User-provided image", licenseStatus "unknown/user-provided".

screens.title: My Mask Leaks or Moves Around

claims.text: My Mask Leaks or Moves Around
claims.ciasQuote: What if air is leaking around the mask or the mask moves around in my sleep?

claims.text: Air leaks may mean intended airflow is escaping.
claims.ciasQuote: It’s important to address this because an air leak means the air might not be reaching your airway and preventing obstruction.
claims.note: The CIAS reason (air may not reach the airway to prevent obstruction; "important to address") is softened. The CIAS tip that you can hear or feel a leak is left out.

claims.text: Check fit and straps.
claims.ciasQuote: You may need to play around with adjusting the straps to ensure a fit where the mask stays in place or prevents a leak.

claims.text: Red or sore eyes after waking can signal air leaking from the top of the mask.
claims.ciasQuote: What if my eyes are red or sore after waking up? | This might be a sign that air is leaking from the top of the mask.
claims.note: Wording matches CIAS. CIAS asks this as its own question on p22; the app merges it into the leak screen.

claims.text: If it persists, another mask style may be needed.
claims.ciasQuote: you find you need to tighten the mask to be extremely tight to keep a seal, then a different style of mask might be necessary.

claims.text: While the machine is running, lift the mask slightly away from your face and let it reseal, then adjust the headgear gradually.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: Check that the cushion is not folded and that the tubing and connectors are seated.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: Reduce tugging by routing the tubing over your chest or using a tubing holder.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: A pillow designed with space for the mask may help some side sleepers.
claims.ciasQuote: Other suggestions would be to buy a CPAP pillow that helps positioning.
claims.note: CIAS: a CPAP pillow "helps positioning"; app narrows it to side sleepers.

claims.text: Persistent leaks or eye irritation deserve a mask-fit review.
claims.ciasQuote: Talk to your healthcare provider about trying a different mask style. | Click here to learn more about different CPAP mask styles. Learn more about ensuring proper mask fit.

claims.text: A good seal should not require blocking the mask vents or tightening until your skin hurts.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p21
claims.ciasQuote: you find you need to tighten the mask to be extremely tight to keep a seal, then a different style of mask might be necessary.
claims.note: Vent-blocking warning is not in CIAS. CIAS threshold is "extremely tight"; app says "until your skin hurts".

claims.text: Bring repeated leaks, red eyes, or frequent mask movement to the PAP team.
claims.ciasQuote: Talk to your healthcare provider about trying a different mask style.

screens.narrationNote: EN narrationText equals paragraphs + keyPoints, in order, word for word. ES narrationText also matches its own visible text.
mediaNotes: image-registry m9-03-mask-leak-illustration.jpg: illustration of a full-face mask with airflow at the sides; alt text accurate; license unknown/user-provided.

screens.title: There Is Water in My Mask or I Hear Whistling

claims.text: There Is Water in My Mask or I Hear Whistling
claims.ciasQuote: What if water is leaking out of my mask or I hear a whistling noise?

claims.text: Condensation can occur with too much humidification or a large temperature difference between tubing and surrounding air.
claims.ciasQuote: There might be too much humidification causing water to condense (which can also cause whistling sounds). | If there is a big temperature difference between the tube and the surrounding air, this can also increase water condensation.

claims.text: Use supported humidification and tubing-warming controls as directed for comfort.
claims.ciasQuote: You can try a “tube cozy” to warm the area around the tube.
claims.note: CIAS: a "tube cozy". App: "tubing-warming controls", which implies heated-tubing features CIAS does not mention.

claims.text: If water collects, try lowering the heated-humidifier setting
claims.ciasQuote: Try turning down the setting or switching back to “auto” if on a fixed setting.
claims.note: CIAS alternative "switching back to auto if on a fixed setting" is omitted.

claims.text: warming the room
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p21
claims.ciasQuote: If there is a big temperature difference between the tube and the surrounding air, this can also increase water condensation.
claims.note: Follows logically from the CIAS temperature-difference point but is not stated.

claims.text: insulating the tubing
claims.ciasQuote: You can try a “tube cozy” to warm the area around the tube.
claims.note: = "tube cozy".

claims.text: using heated PAP tubing when your device supports it
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: Change one setting at a time and follow the device manual.
claims.note: App-authored process guidance.

claims.text: A whistle can come from a small leak, a loose connection, or a vent or cushion that needs checking.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p21
claims.ciasQuote: There might be too much humidification causing water to condense (which can also cause whistling sounds).
claims.note: CIAS says whistling can come from condensation caused by too much humidification. The app gives leak, connection, vent or cushion causes and does not mention the CIAS one. Not a direct contradiction, but the CIAS cause is lost.

claims.text: Do not cover the intentional exhalation vents; ask the equipment team to inspect unusual sounds that persist.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: Water in the tubing is often called rainout and can improve when tubing and room temperatures are closer.
claims.ciasQuote: If there is a big temperature difference between the tube and the surrounding air, this can also increase water condensation.
claims.note: The term "rainout" is app-added.

claims.text: Use only the humidification and tubing options supported by your machine.
claims.note: App-authored.

screens.title: My Skin Is Irritated

claims.text: My Skin Is Irritated
claims.ciasQuote: What if my skin around the mask is irritated or I may be having an allergic reaction?
claims.note: "Allergic reaction" is dropped from the title but covered in P1.

claims.text: Persistent irritation may relate to mask contact, fit, or material.
claims.ciasQuote: Make sure you have a hypoallergenic mask made of silicone.
claims.note: Material angle implied by CIAS hypoallergenic-silicone point.

claims.text: If it continues or a reaction is suspected, discuss another interface or mask option with the healthcare provider or equipment team.
claims.ciasQuote: If you experience a reaction to the mask cushion, talk to your healthcare provider about trying a different type of mask.

claims.text: Check that the mask is secure but not painfully tight.
claims.ciasQuote: The mask should not be too tight on the face or leave long lasting facial marks in the morning after nightly use.
claims.note: CIAS states this in the mask-comfort question (p21), not the skin question. Same "painfully" threshold drift as m9-02.

claims.text: Clean and dry your face and mask components according to the manufacturer instructions; skin oils or residue can interfere with the seal.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: Ask about a different size or style, a mask liner, or another approved cushion if rubbing continues.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p22
claims.ciasQuote: If you experience a reaction to the mask cushion, talk to your healthcare provider about trying a different type of mask.
claims.note: A different style is supported. The mask liner and "approved cushion" are not in CIAS. The CIAS fix for friction (petroleum creams) is not offered.

claims.text: An open sore, spreading redness, or worsening reaction needs prompt review by a healthcare professional.
claims.note: Safety-net thresholds are app-authored.

claims.text: Treat persistent skin injury as a fit or skin-care problem to review, not something to push through.
claims.note: App-authored.

claims.text: Do not apply an unapproved product to the mask or skin without checking the manufacturer or care team.
claims.ciasQuote: You can also use petroleum creams (e.g., Vaseline, Aquaphor) to help reduce friction on your face.
claims.note: Implied conflict: CIAS suggests petroleum creams (Vaseline, Aquaphor) on the face to reduce friction. The app leaves that out and instead warns against unapproved products without checking first. Not a literal contradiction, but the default advice points the opposite way. Clinical reviewer to decide; not settled here.

screens.narrationNote: EN narrationText equals paragraphs + keyPoints, in order, word for word. ES narrationText also matches its own visible text.
spanishNotes: "esté segura" for "secure" can be read as "safe"; minor wording only.

claims.ciasQuote: What if my eyes are red or sore after waking up? | This might be a sign that air is leaking from the top of the mask.

claims.ciasQuote: only a physician can determine the pressure amount needed
claims.note: Distractor. CIAS supports it being wrong (only a physician sets pressure).

claims.text: Check the mask fit and seek mask support if the leak continues.
claims.ciasQuote: This might be a sign that air is leaking from the top of the mask. | Talk to your healthcare provider about trying a different mask style.

claims.text: Stop PAP altogether because any eye irritation means the treatment is unsafe.
claims.ciasQuote: try to use your CPAP every time you sleep

claims.text: Increase humidification before checking whether air is leaking.
claims.ciasQuote: This might be a sign that air is leaking from the top of the mask.

claims.text: c2
claims.ciasQuote: This might be a sign that air is leaking from the top of the mask. | Talk to your healthcare provider about trying a different mask style.
claims.note: Supported by CIAS p22/p21 and by m9-03. Not debatable.

claims.text: Air near the top of the mask can indicate a leak. Check fit first and seek mask support if it persists.
claims.ciasQuote: This might be a sign that air is leaking from the top of the mask.

claims.text: Correct. / Not quite.

screens.title: My Nose or Mouth Feels Dry

claims.text: My Nose or Mouth Feels Dry
claims.ciasQuote: What if my nose/mouth feels dry and uncomfortable?

claims.text: PAP airflow can feel drying.
claims.ciasQuote: In general, CPAP tends to dry out the air and this can be uncomfortable.

claims.text: Nasal saline and PAP humidification may improve comfort, but too much humidity can cause unwanted moisture.
claims.ciasQuote: You can use a nasal saline spray before sleep at night or there are several humidifier options (pass-over humidifier or heated humidifier) | However, too much moisture can also create areas of moisture collection that can be irritating so finding a comfortable balance is key.
claims.note: CIAS humidifier types (pass-over/heated), saline "before sleep" timing, and the extra room-humidifier tip are not carried over.

claims.text: Discuss persistent problems with the healthcare or equipment team.
claims.note: Generic referral; the CIAS dryness answer has none.

claims.text: Check for a mask or mouth leak first, especially if you use a nasal mask or nasal pillows.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen. Leak-first ordering not in CIAS.

claims.text: If your device has humidification, ask whether a higher heat setting or heated tubing is appropriate; balance comfort against condensation.
claims.ciasQuote: Humidification can usually be controlled with the newer CPAP devices. | However, too much moisture can also create areas of moisture collection that can be irritating so finding a comfortable balance is key.
claims.note: Balance point supported. Heated tubing is app-added. CIAS treats humidification as something you can adjust yourself; the app says to ask first.

claims.text: Saline spray or gel can help some people with nasal dryness, and artificial-saliva products may help some people with dry mouth.
claims.ciasQuote: You can use a nasal saline spray before sleep at night or there are several humidifier options (pass-over humidifier or heated humidifier) | Other options include oral sprays such as Kote Dry Mouth Spray or Biotene spray.
claims.note: CIAS brand names (Kote, Biotene) made generic. "Gel" is app-added.

claims.text: Ask the care team before adding a chin strap or changing mask type.
claims.ciasQuote: Sometimes a chin strap or mouth tape like Somnofix can help keep your mouth closed, helping with the sensation of dry mouth.
claims.note: CIAS lists the chin strap under the mouth-open question without a check-first step (check-first applies only to mouth tape). The app adds caution.

claims.text: Dryness can be a clue to a leak, not only a need for more humidity.
claims.note: App-authored or from ATS supplement (pending clinical approval); grouped in clinicalReview for this screen.

claims.text: Change humidification gradually and record whether dryness or condensation improves.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p22
claims.ciasQuote: However, too much moisture can also create areas of moisture collection that can be irritating so finding a comfortable balance is key.
claims.note: Balance idea supported; the gradual-change and record-keeping method is app-added.

screens.narrationNote: EN narrationText equals paragraphs + keyPoints, in order, word for word. ES narrationText also matches its own visible text.
spanishNotes: "demasiada humedad puede causar humedad no deseada" ("too much humidity can cause unwanted humidity") is circular; EN says "unwanted moisture". Meaning kept.

screens.title: My Mouth Opens While I Sleep

claims.text: My Mouth Opens While I Sleep
claims.ciasQuote: What if my mouth is open while I sleep and I am having dry mouth?

claims.text: Persistent mouth opening may contribute to dry mouth and PAP problems.
claims.ciasQuote: What if my mouth is open while I sleep and I am having dry mouth?

claims.text: A full-face mask may be needed for some people; the prescribing healthcare team can help troubleshoot.
claims.ciasQuote: To ensure CPAP pressure is optimal, you may need to get a full-face mask. | Talk to the healthcare provider that prescribed your CPAP machine to help you troubleshoot these issues.
claims.note: CIAS reason "to ensure CPAP pressure is optimal" is omitted.

claims.text: When a nasal mask or nasal pillows are used, mouth opening can let air escape and dry the mouth.
claims.note: Mechanism is app-added; consistent with CIAS.

claims.text: Nasal congestion can make this more likely, so address congestion as part of the troubleshooting conversation.
claims.ciasLocator: ABSENT as stated; related context p22
claims.ciasQuote: We would not recommend using a mouth tape without checking with your doctor to ensure that your nasal passages are healthy.
claims.note: CIAS links nasal health only to mouth-tape safety.

claims.text: Ask the care team whether a chin strap or a clinician-fitted full-face mask is appropriate.
claims.ciasQuote: Sometimes a chin strap or mouth tape like Somnofix can help keep your mouth closed, helping with the sensation of dry mouth.
claims.note: Mouth tape (Somnofix) and the CIAS "check with your doctor" caveat are omitted (see omissions).

claims.text: Mask choice depends on fit, breathing comfort, leak, and your treatment plan.
claims.note: App-authored.

claims.text: Mouth leak is a reason to review the interface, not to tighten every strap.
claims.note: App-authored; consistent with CIAS.

claims.text: Have the PAP team help choose and fit any alternate interface.
claims.ciasQuote: Talk to the healthcare provider that prescribed your CPAP machine to help you troubleshoot these issues.

claims.ciasQuote: What if I am having a “runny nose” (nasal congestion), or my seasonal allergies are worsened by the CPAP? | What if my nose is irritated?
claims.note: Merges two CIAS p23 questions.

claims.text: Keep PAP filters clean.
claims.ciasQuote: Change your CPAP filters often
claims.note: CIAS: "change ... often"; app: "keep clean" (P3 adds replace/clean per manual).

claims.text: Use humidifier and heat options according to device setup and comfort
claims.ciasQuote: Try the CPAP humidifier with and without heat to see which is most comfortable for you

claims.text: and use distilled water as directed.
claims.ciasQuote: Use distilled water in the CPAP humidifier and change it daily
claims.note: "Change it daily" is not stated here; it is covered by the m9-11 empty-each-morning routine (ORGANIZATIONAL).

claims.text: and discuss medications or persistent symptoms with the healthcare provider.

claims.ciasQuote: Try using a humidifier, preferably a heated one. Use a saline spray before sleep.

Please speak to your healthcare provider prior to starting. | is safe to use in pregnancy and we would recommend using that as a first option. | Nasal steroids are also safe to use in pregnancy and some are found over the counter.

claims.ciasQuote: Change your CPAP filters often

screens.title: I’m Burping or Feeling Bloated

claims.text: I’m Burping or Feeling Bloated
claims.ciasQuote: What if I’m burping a lot or feeling bloated?

claims.text: Burping or bloating may be a sign of swallowing air.
claims.ciasQuote: That could be a sign you are swallowing air (going down your esophagus) instead of your trachea (windpipe).
claims.note: The esophagus-vs-windpipe explanation is omitted.

claims.text: Some PAP devices have a ramp feature that reduces pressure while falling asleep.
claims.ciasQuote: Some CPAP machines have a “ramp feature” that helps reduce the pressure that the device delivers while you’re falling asleep.

claims.text: Discuss pressure changes with the healthcare provider rather than making them independently.
claims.ciasQuote: Speak to your healthcare provider to adjust your CPAP pressure and keep the head of the bed up if you can. | only a physician can determine the pressure amount needed

claims.text: Changing your sleeping position or pillow arrangement may help some people.
claims.ciasQuote: Speak to your healthcare provider to adjust your CPAP pressure and keep the head of the bed up if you can.
claims.note: The specific CIAS advice "keep the head of the bed up if you can" is made more general (see omissions).

claims.text: If available on your device, a ramp can lower the starting pressure while you fall asleep; ask the care team how to use it.
claims.ciasQuote: Some CPAP machines have a “ramp feature” that helps reduce the pressure that the device delivers while you’re falling asleep.

claims.text: Persistent, painful, or worsening bloating needs prompt review of the mask, pressure, and device mode.
claims.note: Safety-net threshold is app-authored.

screens.title: Cleaning PAP Equipment

claims.text: Cleaning PAP Equipment
claims.ciasQuote: How often should I clean the CPAP machine? | How do I clean my CPAP machine?
claims.note: Merges two CIAS questions: how often to clean (p23-24) and how to clean (p24).

claims.text: Follow the manufacturer’s instructions first.
claims.ciasQuote: Check your machine’s manual for instructions on cleaning and frequency. | Check your machine’s manual for instructions on cleaning.

claims.text: Compatible general guidance includes mild soap, thorough rinsing, and air drying relevant mask and humidifier components,
claims.ciasQuote: Detach the mask and wash the surfaces with mild soap, rinse, and allow to air dry (outside of direct sunlight). | regular cleaning of the mask and humidifier components daily, and tubing on a weekly basis is recommended to promote your health and machine longevity.
claims.note: The method matches CIAS, but the CIAS frequency for mask and humidifier components ("daily") is dropped.

claims.text: with weekly tubing cleaning
claims.ciasQuote: regular cleaning of the mask and humidifier components daily, and tubing on a weekly basis is recommended to promote your health and machine longevity.

claims.text: and periodic broader cleaning
claims.ciasQuote: All of the components of your machine should be sanitized at least once a month.
claims.note: CIAS says to sanitize all components at least once a month. "Periodic" loses that minimum. The CIAS sanitizing method (vinegar soak) is also omitted.

claims.text: as recommended by the CIAS source.

claims.note: CIAS says "always". The boiled-and-cooled water alternative and the mineral-deposit fallback are omitted.

claims.text: A practical routine is to empty the humidifier chamber each morning, refill it with fresh distilled water before sleep,
claims.ciasQuote: Use distilled water in the CPAP humidifier and change it daily | Replace the water in the humidification chamber. Wash with soap. Allow to air dry outside of direct sunlight.

claims.note: Leaves the frequency to the manual; CIAS says daily.

claims.text: Wash mask parts, tubing, and headgear with warm water and mild soap on the schedule supplied with your device, then rinse and air-dry away from direct heat or sunlight.
claims.ciasQuote: Detach the mask and wash the surfaces with mild soap, rinse, and allow to air dry (outside of direct sunlight). | Remove the tubing and wash with mild soap, rinse well, and allow to air dry over a shower rod.

clinicalReview.issue: All 14 m9 screens, including the 3 quizzes, list the same sourceIds: cias-ez-pap-document plus ats-pap-overview, ats-pap-troubleshooting and ats-pap-care-cleaning. The repo docs (CLINICAL_SOURCE_REGISTRY.md, CIAS_SOURCE_TRACEABILITY.md) say the three ATS IDs are not yet clinically approved, and there is no statement-level mapping. Every NOT_IN_CIAS instruction in this audit depends on those unapproved sources or is app-authored. Context: CIAS itself lists the ATS PAP troubleshooting PDF under "Section IV: Resources to Incorporate or Link to" (p27). That may bear on approving ats-pap-troubleshooting, but not the other two.

Threshold drift: CIAS says the mask should not be "too tight" and, if it must be "very tight", to ask the healthcare provider about a different type of mask. The app says "painfully tight" and "ask for a refit". App-added fitting technique (fit with airflow on, one strap at a time, overtightening worsens leaks) is not in CIAS.
App-added leak technique not in CIAS: lift-and-reseal with airflow on, checking for a folded cushion and seated connectors, routing tubing over the chest or using a holder, not blocking vents.

Whistling cause differs: CIAS says whistling can come from condensation caused by too much humidification; the app gives leak, connection, vent and cushion causes and never states the CIAS cause. Heated-tubing advice and the vent warning are not in CIAS. Omitted CIAS tips: switch to "auto", and put the machine on the floor (which conflicts with the CIAS p23 advice to lift it away from dust).

CONTRADICTION (implied): CIAS p22 suggests petroleum creams (Vaseline, Aquaphor) on the face to reduce friction. m9-05 leaves this out and says "Do not apply an unapproved product to the mask or skin without checking the manufacturer or care team." CIAS "hypoallergenic mask made of silicone" is omitted. The mask liner, face/mask cleaning for seal, and skin safety-net thresholds are not in CIAS.

App-added: check for a leak first, heated tubing, saline gel, and asking before a chin strap. CIAS treats humidification as something the user adjusts; the app says to ask first. Omitted: extra room humidifier, humidifier types.
CIAS offers mouth tape (Somnofix) with a "check with your doctor" caveat; the app leaves both out. A clinical decision is needed on whether the omission is intentional.

PREGNANCY-SPECIFIC: CIAS p23 says saline spray is safe in pregnancy and the recommended first option, nasal steroids are also safe in pregnancy (some are over the counter), and both are preferred to oral medicines. m9-08 leaves all of this out and adds "especially during pregnancy" as a caution. App-added thresholds: nosebleeds, worsening breathing. If the CIAS nostril-cream advice is restored, its self-contradiction (non-petroleum cream vs Vaseline) needs resolving.

App-added therapy content not in CIAS Section III: the clinician may consider an expiratory comfort feature, auto-PAP or bilevel PAP (CIAS p10 lists these only as prescriber-chosen machine types), and the "prompt review" threshold. The specific CIAS advice "keep the head of the bed up if you can" is made more general.
App-added: heated tube, and routing tubing over the chest or under a blanket to reduce heat loss. Not in CIAS.

Cleaning frequency and method are blurred against CIAS p24, which says: mask and humidifier components daily; tubing weekly; humidifier sanitized weekly with 1:1 white vinegar and water for 15-20 minutes; all components sanitized at least once a month (20-minute vinegar soak); always distilled or boiled-and-cooled water. The app keeps only "weekly tubing" and leaves the rest to the manufacturer ("periodic broader cleaning"). The ATS-derived bans (immersion, bleach, alcohol, harsh cleaners, household wipes, unapproved cleaning devices) are not in CIAS. A reviewer needs to decide whether to restore the CIAS frequencies and vinegar method within the manufacturer-first framing (CIAS typo "1 white vinegar" if restored).

TRAVEL and FLYING: the CIAS p24 questions "How do I continue CPAP if I'm traveling?" (travel or battery machines, RV power) and "Can I fly with a CPAP machine?" (carry-on or checked luggage, removal for x-ray screening, TSA links) are not in m9. In the whole app, only m8 has a brief "including ... travel" line. This is CIAS-sourced content, not new advice; the decision whether to add it belongs to the content owner or clinical reviewer.

Other Section III content is omitted (rental and insurance, mask-style/fit/humidity links, CPAP can worsen allergies, lift the machine away from dust, pets and vacuuming, oral allergy medicine, esophagus explanation). See the omissions list. The reviewer should decide which to restore.
